newsitem.title: USA: Dole stumps hard, slams Clinton on ethics. [CORRECTED 10:51 GMT 03/11]
newsitem.headline: Dole stumps hard, slams Clinton on ethics. [CORRECTED 10:51 GMT 03/11]

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole charged through the second hectic day of his campaign-ending marathon on Saturday, vowing to win the race and still chipper despite a sleep-deprived schedule.
"We are going to win this election," said Dole at a sunrise breakfast outside Philadelphia.

He said he intended to finish his campaign in Independence, Missouri, the hometown of Harry Truman -- a Democrat -- who came from behind to win the 1948 presidential race. "We're going to do it again ... a second Harry Truman," Dole said. "We're going to make it happen."
In Indianapolis later, Dole said ethical questions surrounding the administration of President Bill Clinton were starting to take hold with the voting public and swinging momentum Dole's way.

"We've had literally a scandal a week in this administration the past several weeks. I think the American people are starting to say 'what's going on there? What's going on in this White House?'" he said.

Dole is lagging Clinton in the polls ahead of Tuesday's election but, cheered by recent polls showing the gap narrowing, hopes his marathon tactics will inject enthusiasm into his campaign and swing voters to his side.

In the Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll released on Saturday, Dole had closed the gap between him and Clinton to 3.8 percentage points -- 42.4 percent to 38.6 percent, with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot at 8.4 percent. Other polls, however, show Clinton with a much larger margin.
Commenting on new polls, Dole told reporters on his plane, "I think it's moving in our direction."
"I think its tightening up everywhere. A lot of good numbers floating around. A lot of polls out tomorrow," he said.
At the breakfast in Essington, Pennsylvania, retired Gen. Colin Powell offered his own confident prediction of success.

"It's a race ... that is winnable and he's going to win it," Powell, who was chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff, told a crowd of several hundred at the Lagoon Restaurant along the Delaware River outside Philadelphia.
Dole told the Indianapolis crowd of 1,500 in an airplane hangar that if Clinton were re-elected his ability to lead would be crippled by investigations into alleged improprieties.
"If he's re-elected he's going to spend half of his time next year with investigations ... who knows what will happen in the next 24 months, 36 months," Dole said.
Dole was in the midst of a second full day of a campaign marathon that will continue until he casts his vote in his hometown of Russell, Kansas, on Tuesday.

On Saturday, he added new stops to his itinerary, bringing to 19 the number of states on his route. He is to campaign all day Sunday in California, then on Monday he goes to Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Iowa.
"Ninety-six hours. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop. Non stop," Dole said at the breakfast.
Dole spoke then about the disorienting effects of the campaign endurance race. "I can't remember when we started, but I can remember where we've been," he said.
On route to Covington, Dole told reporters he had some naps on the plane, bringing his total sleeping time to about 2 1/2 hours since Friday morning.
(Corrects to delete incorrect reference to Covington being a suburb of Indianapolis.)
He said earlier he felt a "little bit" tired. "Not bad, though," he said. "We'll be all right. I'm starting to get used to it."
At a pre-dawn stop in New Jersey, he called out while signing autographs, "I'm in Philadelphia, right?"
Asked how he kept himself going, Dole told reporters, "I drink a lot of liquids, but not a lot of coffee. Eat a lot of fruit. Drink a lot of that water."

Dole's voice sounded tired by the time he reached an afternoon stop in Covington, a suburb of Cincinnati, Ohio. He spoke briefly, and turned the stage over to his wife, Elizabeth, who had flown in to meet him there.
